text: The Cape Hatteras Light is a lighthouse located on Hatteras Island in the Outer Banks of North Carolina, within the town of Buxton and part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore. It is the tallest lighthouse in the United States from base to tip at 210 feet and the tallest brick lighthouse structure in the country at 198 feet, ranking second in the world for brick lighthouse height. Its semi-unique pattern makes it easily recognizable and widely regarded as one of the most beautiful and famous lighthouses in the U.S. The Outer Banks are a group of barrier islands along the North Carolina coast that separate the Atlantic Ocean from coastal sounds and inlets. The area is known as the "Graveyard of the Atlantic" due to dangerous shifting sandbars, particularly near Diamond Shoals off Cape Hatteras, where Atlantic currents and the collision of the warm Gulf Stream with the colder Labrador Current create powerful storms and swells, leading to numerous shipwrecks. This prompted the U.S. Congress to authorize the construction of the lighthouse. The original 1802 structure, built of dark sandstone and standing 112 feet above sea level, had 18 lamps with 14-inch reflectors and was visible up to 18 miles in clear weather. In 1851, Lt. David D. Porter criticized the light as unreliable, noting it was often mistaken for a steamer’s light and could not be trusted to guide vessels. Improvements began in 1845 with 15-inch reflectors, followed by 15 lamps with 21-inch reflectors in 1848, increasing visibility to 20 miles. In 1854, a first-order Fresnel lens with a flashing white light replaced the old system, and the tower was raised to 150 feet. In 1860, the Civil War caused damage to the lighthouse, with the lens and lantern destroyed in 1862. Congress approved $80,000 in 1868 to build a new beacon. Completed in under two years under brevet Brigadier General J. H. Simpson, the new 200-foot-tall brick tower, with a focal height of 208 feet above water, became the tallest brick lighthouse tower in the world and was first lit on December 16, 1871. The old tower was demolished in February 1871 and its ruins were eventually eroded away by a storm in 1980. In 1879, lightning struck the tower, causing cracks that were repaired by connecting the ironwork to an iron disk buried in the ground. In 1912, the candlepower of the light was increased from 27,000 to 80,000. Gradual coastal erosion began in the spring of 1879, becoming severe by 1919 when the high water line reached 120 feet from the base, and by 1935, the surf reached the tower’s base. A steel skeleton tower, the Buxton Woods Tower, was installed in 1935, 166 feet above sea level, visible for 19 miles. The original brick tower was placed under the National Park Service. In 1942, during World War II, the Coast Guard took control of the brick tower as a lookout station until 1945. Due to sand accretion, the tower was 500 to 900 feet inland by then and was reactivated on January 23, 1950, with a 36-inch aviation-type rotating beacon of 250,000 candlepower, flashing every 7.5 seconds and visible 20 miles. The light displays a black and white diagonal daymark scheme, similar to the St. Augustine Light, and shares this pattern with other North Carolina lighthouses to help sailors identify them during daylight. The Coast Guard operates the navigational equipment, while the National Park Service maintains the tower as a historic structure. The lighthouse stands 208 feet from the foundation to the roof, requiring 268 steps to reach the light, which shines 191 feet above mean high-water mark. It was constructed using 1,250,000 bricks. In 1999, due to severe erosion, the lighthouse was moved 2,900 feet (880 meters) to the southwest, placing it 1,500 feet (460 meters) from the current shoreline, as it had only been 15 feet from the water’s edge. All support buildings were relocated while maintaining their original compass orientation and distance/height relationships. The move was awarded to International Chimney Corp. of Buffalo, New York, with assistance from Expert House Movers, and completed on September 14, 1999. The relocation, known as "The Move of the Millennium," was controversial and led to lawsuits that were dismissed. The project earned the 40th Annual Outstanding Civil Engineering Achievement Award from the American Society of Civil Engineers in 1999. The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse is one of the tallest masonry structures ever moved, standing 200 feet tall and weighing 5,000 tons. It continues to serve as an aid to navigation, protecting mariners from the treacherous shoals of the Graveyard of the Atlantic.
